blurbs.A: Easy to find. Fix anything below and keep it that way.
blurbs.B: Mostly findable. A few fixes will help search engines and AI read you right.
blurbs.C: Findable, with gaps. Work through the list, top first.
blurbs.D: Hard to find. Fix the high and medium items before anything else.
blurbs.F: Close to invisible. Start with the first finding.

footer: Rankings, keywords and backlinks aren't in this scan: Google Search Console shows those for your own site, free.

ai-crawlers-blocked.d: Your robots.txt keeps some AI companies' training crawlers out, so your future pages won't be used to train their models. That's a fair choice and we don't score it. It doesn't affect whether assistants can find and cite you when they search; their search crawlers are separate.
ai-crawlers-blocked.v: If you want them in, remove their Disallow lines in robots.txt. If you want them out, nothing to do.

ai-search-blocked.d: Your robots.txt blocks the crawlers AI assistants use to search the web while they answer ({excerpt}). Those assistants can't cite your site, so when someone asks about your category they'll quote other people's pages. It's your call and we don't score it, but it's often left over from a rule meant only for training crawlers.
ai-search-blocked.f: My robots.txt blocks AI search crawlers ({excerpt}). If I only meant to keep my site out of AI training, change it so the training crawlers (GPTBot, ClaudeBot, Google-Extended, Applebot-Extended, CCBot) stay blocked and the search crawlers (OAI-SearchBot, Claude-SearchBot, PerplexityBot) fall through to 'User-agent: *' and are allowed. Also check my host's or CDN's bot settings for an AI crawler block.
ai-search-blocked.v: Open /robots.txt and check no group naming a search crawler has 'Disallow: /'.

canonical-elsewhere.d: These pages tell search engines that a different URL is the real one, so the page itself won't rank. Usually a copied <head> or a hard-coded home page URL.
canonical-elsewhere.f: These pages have a canonical URL that isn't their own address: {excerpt}. Make every page's canonical its own full URL, on the same host form (www or not) the site actually serves.
canonical-elsewhere.v: View source on each page listed and check the canonical matches the address bar.

canonical-missing.d: A canonical tag tells search engines which address is the real one when a page is reachable several ways (with and without www, a trailing slash, tracking parameters). Without it they guess, and can split your ranking between copies.
canonical-missing.f: Add <link rel="canonical" href="..."> to the <head> of every page, pointing at that page's own full URL on my main domain ({excerpt}). Generate it from the route so each page gets its own.
canonical-missing.v: View source on each page and check the canonical is the page's own address.

canonical-ok.t: Canonical URLs point at their own page

csr-generic.d: Your page's raw HTML has almost no text: the content is drawn by JavaScript after it loads. Google renders JavaScript eventually, later and less reliably. ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity and most link previews don't run it at all, so to them your site is an empty page.
csr-generic.f: My site renders its content with client-side JavaScript ({excerpt}), so crawlers get HTML with no text. Make the public pages serve real HTML: prerender them at build time or render them on the server, so each has its own <title>, meta description and visible copy in the HTML that's served. The logged-in app can stay client-side.
csr-generic.v: View source (not Inspect) on the page: your headline and copy should be in the HTML. Then re-run this scan.

csr-next.d: Your page's raw HTML has almost no text: the content is drawn by JavaScript after it loads. Google renders JavaScript eventually, later and less reliably. ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity and most link previews don't run it at all, so to them your site is an empty page.
csr-next.f: My Next.js site ({excerpt}) sends crawlers HTML with no content, because the public pages render on the client. Make the marketing pages server components (remove 'use client' from the page and layout, move interactive bits into small client components), fetch their data on the server, and don't wrap the page in a provider that renders nothing until it mounts. Use static generation for pages that don't change per visitor.
csr-next.v: View source (not Inspect) on the page: your headline and copy should be in the HTML. Then re-run this scan.

csr-vite.d: Your page's raw HTML has almost no text: the content is drawn by JavaScript after it loads. Google renders JavaScript eventually, later and less reliably. ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity and most link previews don't run it at all, so to them your site is an empty page.
csr-vite.f: My site is a client-side Vite + React app ({excerpt}), so crawlers and AI bots get an empty <div id="root"> with no text. Make the public pages (home, pricing, about, each feature page) render real HTML at build time: prerender those routes to static HTML (vite-plugin-prerender, or react-snap), or move the marketing pages to a static site generator, and keep the logged-in app as it is. Every public page should have its own <title>, meta description and visible text in the HTML that's served.
csr-vite.v: Run 'curl -s https://yoursite.com/ | grep -c "<p"' or view source (not Inspect) in your browser: your headline and copy should be in it. Then re-run this scan.

data-files-missing.d: Nothing on the site or in llms.txt links to a data file (JSON, CSV, Markdown). Not needed for most sites; useful when you publish prices, docs or a changelog that an AI should quote exactly.
data-files-missing.f: Publish the facts an AI should get exactly right (plans and prices, a changelog, docs) as a JSON or Markdown file on my site, and link it from llms.txt.
data-files-missing.v: Open llms.txt and check the link to the data file works.

description-duplicate.d: Several pages have the same description, which tells search engines they're the same page.
description-duplicate.f: These pages share a meta description: {excerpt}. Write one for each that describes that page.
description-duplicate.t: Pages share the same meta description

description-length.d: Search results show about 160 characters. A longer description is cut off mid-sentence; a very short one wastes the space.
description-length.f: Rewrite these meta descriptions to 70 to 160 characters: {excerpt}.
description-length.t: Meta descriptions too short or too long

description-missing.d: The meta description is the grey text under your link in search results. Without one, search engines lift a random sentence from the page.
description-missing.f: These pages have no meta description: {excerpt}. Write one per page, 70 to 160 characters, saying who it's for and what they get, in plain words people would search for.
description-missing.v: View source and check each page has <meta name="description">.

descriptions-ok.t: Every page has a meta description

external-host-mixed.d: You link to the same sites by two different addresses (with and without www) in different places. One of each pair redirects, and to a crawler or an AI reading your llms.txt they look like separate sites.
external-host-mixed.f: I link to these sites with both www and bare addresses: {excerpt}. Use the form each site actually serves (the one it doesn't redirect away from) everywhere: page links, llms.txt and structured data.
external-host-mixed.t: Same sites linked with and without www
external-host-mixed.v: Search your source for each domain and check every mention uses the same form.

faq-schema-missing.d: Your page answers questions ({excerpt}) but doesn't mark them up. FAQPage structured data hands search engines and AI the question and answer pairs directly.
faq-schema-missing.f: My page {path} has a question-and-answer section. Add FAQPage JSON-LD with one Question (name) and acceptedAnswer (Answer, text) per item, using the same wording as the page.
faq-schema-missing.t: Questions on the page, no FAQPage schema
faq-schema-missing.v: Paste the page into validator.schema.org and check it finds the FAQPage with every question.

few-internal-links.d: The home page links to very few other pages on the site. Internal links are how crawlers find pages and how they judge which matter.
few-internal-links.f: My home page links to only {excerpt}. Link to my main pages from the navigation and footer, with link text that says what each page is.

fragment-sections.d: Each part of your offer lives at a #section of one page rather than at its own URL. Search engines ignore everything after #, so one URL can only rank once: none of these sections can be the page that answers a search for it, and an AI can't cite or link one.
fragment-sections.f: My site keeps {excerpt}. Give each important section its own page with its own URL, <title>, meta description and H1 (for example /products/name), keep a short summary on the home page linking to it, and add the new pages to the sitemap.
fragment-sections.v: Each section should have its own address you can paste into Google's URL Inspection, and appear in /sitemap.xml.

h1-missing.d: The H1 is the page's headline as far as search engines are concerned. Without one, they lean on the title alone.
h1-missing.f: These pages have no <h1>: {excerpt}. Give each page one H1 that says plainly what the page offers, using the words a customer would search for.
h1-missing.v: View source and check each page has one <h1>.

h1-multiple.d: More than one H1 blurs what the page is about.
h1-multiple.f: These pages have more than one <h1>: {excerpt}. Keep one H1 for the page's main headline and make the rest H2s.
h1-multiple.t: Pages with more than one H1

h1-off-topic.d: Your H1 shares no words with your title or description. A clever headline is fine for people, but search engines and AI read the H1 to learn what the page is about, and these words aren't telling them.
h1-off-topic.f: My home page H1 ({excerpt}) doesn't say what the product is. Keep the voice, but work in the category words people search for (what it is and who it's for), the same words my title and description use.
h1-off-topic.t: The headline doesn't say what you sell
h1-off-topic.v: Read the H1 aloud to someone who's never seen the site: can they say what you sell?

heading-skip.d: Headings jump a level (an H1 followed by an H3). Crawlers and screen readers use heading levels as the page's outline.
heading-skip.f: Fix the heading order on these pages so each level follows the one above it (H1, then H2, then H3): {excerpt}. Change the tag, not the look; style with CSS.

home-noindex.d: Your home page says noindex ({excerpt}). Google and Bing will drop it from results, and AI assistants that search the web won't find it either. This is usually a staging setting that shipped to production.
home-noindex.f: My home page is marked noindex ({excerpt}). Find where that's set (a <meta name="robots" content="noindex"> in the layout, a robots setting in the framework's metadata, or an X-Robots-Tag header in the host config or middleware) and remove it for production, keeping it only on preview and staging deployments.
home-noindex.t: The home page tells search engines not to index it
home-noindex.v: View the page source and the response headers of the live home page: neither should say noindex. Then ask Google to recrawl it in Search Console.

host-duplicate.d: Both addresses answer with the full site instead of one redirecting to the other. Search engines see two copies, split links between them and pick one to show, maybe not the one you'd choose.
host-duplicate.f: My site answers on both {excerpt} without redirecting. Pick one (the one my canonical tags use) and make the other return a permanent 301 or 308 redirect to the same path on it. On Vercel or Netlify, set the other domain to redirect in the domain settings.
host-duplicate.t: www and bare domain both serve the site
host-duplicate.v: Run 'curl -sI https://<the other form>/' and check for a 301 or 308 with a Location header on your main domain.

host-ok.t: One form of the domain redirects to the other

host-redirect-temporary.d: One form of your domain redirects to the other with a temporary (302 or 307) redirect. Search engines keep the old address in mind for a temporary one, so links to it don't fully count.
host-redirect-temporary.f: My domain redirects between www and the bare domain with a temporary redirect ({excerpt}). Make it permanent: 301 or 308.
host-redirect-temporary.v: Run 'curl -sI' on the redirecting address and check the status is 301 or 308.

host-unreachable.d: People type www (or leave it off) out of habit. {excerpt} doesn't load at all, so they get an error instead of your site.
host-unreachable.f: {excerpt} doesn't load. Add it as a domain on my host with a DNS record pointing at it, and have it redirect permanently (301 or 308) to my main domain.
host-unreachable.t: The other form of your domain doesn't load
host-unreachable.v: Open the other form in a browser: it should land on your site.

http-not-redirected.d: Your site loads over plain http:// without sending visitors to https://. Browsers mark it 'Not secure', and search engines may index the insecure copy.
http-not-redirected.f: My site serves pages over plain HTTP ({excerpt}). Redirect every http:// request permanently (301 or 308) to the same path on https://, and add a Strict-Transport-Security header.
http-not-redirected.t: Plain HTTP doesn't redirect to HTTPS
http-not-redirected.v: Open http:// plus your domain: the address bar should end on https://.

img-alt-missing.d: Alt text is what search engines and screen readers know about an image. Images without it can't rank in image search and say nothing to people who can't see them.
img-alt-missing.f: Add alt text to these images: {excerpt}. Describe what each shows in a few words. Purely decorative images get alt="" (empty), not no alt.

img-oversized.d: These images are over 300 KB. Large images slow the page, and speed is part of how Google ranks it, especially on phones.
img-oversized.f: These images on my site are over 300 KB: {excerpt}. Resize them to the largest size they're displayed at, convert them to WebP or AVIF, and serve responsive sizes with srcset. Lazy-load anything below the fold.
img-oversized.v: Re-run this scan, or check the images in PageSpeed Insights.

internal-link-redirects.d: Links between your own pages go to an address that redirects. Every one costs a crawler an extra request and some of the link's value.
internal-link-redirects.f: My site links to its own pages at addresses that redirect: {excerpt}. Change those links to the final address (usually a trailing slash or the www/bare form).
internal-link-redirects.v: Re-run this scan; the links should no longer be listed.

internal-links-other-host.d: Some links to your own pages use the other form of your domain (www or bare), so every click and crawl goes through a redirect, and the links point at an address you don't want indexed.
internal-links-other-host.f: Some of my internal links use the other host form: {excerpt}. Use relative links, or the same host my canonical tags use.
internal-links-other-host.t: Internal links use the other host form
internal-links-other-host.v: Re-run this scan; the links should no longer be listed.

jsonld-invalid.d: A JSON-LD block on your site isn't valid JSON, so search engines and AI ignore all of it.
jsonld-invalid.f: A JSON-LD block on {path} isn't valid JSON ({excerpt}). Fix the syntax (usually a trailing comma or an unescaped quote) and build the block with JSON.stringify rather than by hand.
jsonld-invalid.v: Paste the page into validator.schema.org and check it reports no errors.

jsonld-missing.d: Structured data (JSON-LD) states in a machine-readable way who you are, what you sell and what it costs. Search engines use it for rich results; AI assistants use it to get facts like prices right.
jsonld-missing.f: My home page has no JSON-LD structured data. Add a <script type="application/ld+json"> block with an Organization (name, url, logo, sameAs links to my social and directory profiles) and, for what I sell, a SoftwareApplication or Product with an Offer (price, priceCurrency). Use only facts that are true and visible on the page.
jsonld-missing.v: Paste the page into Google's Rich Results Test or validator.schema.org and check it finds your Organization and Product.

lang-missing.d: Without <html lang>, search engines and screen readers have to guess the page's language, and can show it to the wrong audience.
lang-missing.f: Add a lang attribute to the <html> tag on every page ({excerpt}), for example <html lang="en-GB">.
lang-missing.v: View source and check the first tag reads <html lang="...">.

llms-incomplete.d: Your llms.txt exists but doesn't follow the usual shape, so an AI reading it gets less out of it.
llms-incomplete.f: My /llms.txt is missing {excerpt}. It should open with '# ' and the product name, then a '> ' line summarising what it does and for whom, then lists of Markdown links to my key pages with a short note on each.
llms-incomplete.t: llms.txt is missing a summary or links
llms-incomplete.v: Open /llms.txt and check it has the heading, the '> ' summary and links.

llms-missing.d: llms.txt is a short plain-text summary of your site for AI assistants: what it is, who it's for, and links to the pages that matter. It's a new convention, cheap to add, and gives an AI something accurate to quote.
llms-missing.f: Create /llms.txt at my site root, in Markdown: a '# ' heading with the product name, a '> ' line saying in one sentence what it does and for whom, then '## ' sections with links to my key pages (pricing, features, docs, contact), each with a short description. State prices and plans plainly. Serve it as text/plain.
llms-missing.v: Open /llms.txt in a browser: it should be plain text starting with '# ', not your app's home page.

llms-ok.t: llms.txt is there, with a summary and links

offer-missing.d: Your structured data lists products or apps without an Offer, so the price you show on the page isn't machine-readable. AI assistants comparing prices will look elsewhere, or guess.
offer-missing.f: My JSON-LD lists these without an Offer: {excerpt}. Add an 'offers' to each: {{"@type": "Offer", "price": "15", "priceCurrency": "GBP"}}, or an AggregateOffer with lowPrice and highPrice when there are several plans. Use the prices shown on the page.
offer-missing.t: Products without prices in the structured data
offer-missing.v: Paste the page into Google's Rich Results Test and check each product shows its price.

og-image-broken.d: Your og:image points at an image that doesn't load, so every shared link shows a blank space where the picture should be.
og-image-broken.f: My og:image ({excerpt}) doesn't load. Point it at a full https:// URL of an image that exists, 1200x630, PNG or JPEG.
og-image-broken.v: Open the og:image URL in a browser, then check a preview at opengraph.xyz.

og-image-size.d: Link previews are drawn at 1200x630 (1.91:1). Another shape gets cropped or shown as a small thumbnail.
og-image-size.f: My og:image is {excerpt}. Make a 1200x630 version and point og:image at it, with og:image:width and og:image:height set.
og-image-size.t: Link preview image is the wrong shape

og-incomplete.d: Open Graph and Twitter tags decide what a shared link looks like on LinkedIn, Slack, X, WhatsApp and iMessage. Missing ones give a bare URL with no picture.
og-incomplete.f: These pages are missing link-preview tags: {excerpt}. Add them to each page's <head>: og:title, og:description, og:url (the page's own full URL), og:image (a full URL to a 1200x630 image) and twitter:card set to summary_large_image. Generate them from the same title and description the page already uses.
og-incomplete.v: Paste the URL into opengraph.xyz or LinkedIn's Post Inspector.

org-incomplete.d: Your Organization structured data is missing {excerpt}. sameAs (links to your profiles elsewhere) is how search engines and AI connect your site to the rest of your presence.
org-incomplete.f: My Organization JSON-LD is missing {excerpt}. Add them: name, url, logo (full image URL) and sameAs as an array of full URLs to my profiles (LinkedIn, X, GitHub, Product Hunt, Crunchbase). Only list profiles that exist.
org-incomplete.v: Paste the page into validator.schema.org and check the fields appear.

org-missing.d: Your structured data doesn't say who's behind the site. An Organization entry ties your name, logo and profiles together, which helps search engines and AI recognise you as one entity.
org-missing.f: Add an Organization to my JSON-LD with name, url, logo (a full image URL) and sameAs: the full URLs of my profiles elsewhere (LinkedIn, X, GitHub, Product Hunt, Crunchbase).
org-missing.t: No Organization in the structured data
org-missing.v: Paste the page into validator.schema.org and check the Organization shows those fields.

positioning-audience-sprawl.d: The home page addresses {excerpt}. Each extra audience waters down the words the others search with, and an AI asked about one of them finds a page that's half about someone else.
positioning-audience-sprawl.f: My home page tries to speak to {excerpt}. Keep the home page about the main audience, and give each of the others its own page with its own title, H1 and copy in their words, linked from the home page.
positioning-audience-sprawl.t: One page talking to too many audiences
positioning-audience-sprawl.v: Read the home page as each audience: is it obviously for you?

positioning-clear.t: Says what it is and who it's for

positioning-cta-unclear.d: A page that asks for several things at once, or nothing, loses people between reading and doing. {excerpt}
positioning-cta-unclear.f: My home page doesn't have one clear main action ({excerpt}). Pick the one thing a new visitor should do, make it the only primary button above the fold with a label that says what happens ("Start free", "Book a demo"), and turn the other asks into secondary links.
positioning-cta-unclear.t: No single main call to action
positioning-cta-unclear.v: Count the primary buttons on the first screen: there should be one.

positioning-differentiator-ok.t: Says why it beats the alternative

positioning-no-differentiator.d: Comparison questions ("cheaper alternative to X", "X vs Y") are how people ask assistants about products. A page that never says how it differs from a named alternative gives them nothing to quote. {excerpt}
positioning-no-differentiator.f: My home page doesn't say why to choose it over the alternatives ({excerpt}). Write one or two sentences, true and specific, that name what people use instead (a competitor, a spreadsheet, an agency) and the concrete difference: price, commission, time saved, what it does that they don't. No superlatives. Then suggest where on the page they should go.
positioning-no-differentiator.t: No reason to pick you over the alternatives
positioning-no-differentiator.v: Ask: would a reader be able to say how this differs from the thing they use now?

positioning-no-price.d: People asking an AI for a tool usually have a budget, and an answer that can't say what you cost tends to recommend someone who says. {excerpt}
positioning-no-price.f: My home page doesn't state a price ({excerpt}). Add one plain line near the top saying what it costs ("£12 a month, one plan" or "free, no paid plans"), link it to the pricing page, and make the same price machine-readable as an Offer in my JSON-LD.
positioning-no-price.v: Read the first screen of the home page: is a price, or 'free', on it?

positioning-no-social-proof.d: Testimonials, customer names, counts and ratings tell a stranger, and an AI deciding what to recommend, that real people use this. {excerpt}
positioning-no-social-proof.f: My home page has no social proof ({excerpt}). Suggest where to add it and what kind fits my stage: a real quote from a user with their name and role, a count I can stand behind, a rating from a review site, or logos of customers who've agreed. Never invent any of it; if I have none yet, write the email I could send early users to ask for a quote.
positioning-no-social-proof.v: Look for a named person or a number on the home page that shows someone uses it.

positioning-price-ok.t: A price is in the copy

positioning-unclear.d: Someone landing on your home page, or an AI summarising it, should be able to say what you make and who it's for from the title, headline and first lines alone. Here they can't: {excerpt}
positioning-unclear.f: Rewrite my home page's title, H1 and first paragraph so a stranger can say in one sentence what the product is and who it's for. The review said: {excerpt} Name the category in plain words ("booking software for dog groomers", not "reimagine your workflow"), name the audience, and keep my voice. Give me three options for the H1 and one for the opening paragraph.
positioning-unclear.t: A stranger can't tell what it is or who it's for
positioning-unclear.v: Show the top of the page to someone who's never seen it for five seconds, then ask what it is and who it's for.

product-schema-missing.d: Your page shows prices, but nothing in the structured data describes what's being sold. A SoftwareApplication or Product with an Offer makes the price machine-readable.
product-schema-missing.f: My page shows prices but has no SoftwareApplication or Product in its JSON-LD. Add one per thing I sell, with name, description, url and offers ({{"@type": "Offer", "price": ..., "priceCurrency": ...}}), matching the prices on the page.
product-schema-missing.t: Prices on the page, none in the structured data
product-schema-missing.v: Paste the page into Google's Rich Results Test and check it finds the product and its price.

redirect-chain.d: Getting to your page takes more than one redirect. Each hop slows the first visit and crawlers give up on long chains.
redirect-chain.f: These addresses take more than one redirect to reach my site: {excerpt}. Make each redirect go straight to the final https:// URL on my main domain in one hop.
redirect-chain.v: Run 'curl -sIL' on each address and count the Location lines: one at most.

robots-blocks-search.d: Your robots.txt tells Google and Bing not to crawl your home page. They will drop the site from results, or show it with no description. This is usually a leftover from a staging setting.
robots-blocks-search.f: My robots.txt blocks search engines from my site ({excerpt}). Change it so search engines may crawl everything public: 'User-agent: *' then 'Allow: /', and keep Disallow lines only for private areas like /admin. Add a 'Sitemap:' line with my sitemap's full URL. If my host or framework generates robots.txt (Next.js app/robots.ts, a Vercel or Netlify setting), fix it there.
robots-blocks-search.v: Open /robots.txt in a browser and read it. Then paste your home page into Google Search Console's URL Inspection and check 'Crawl allowed? Yes'.

robots-blocks-us.d: robots.txt disallows our crawler, so we only read the crawl files (robots.txt, sitemap.xml, llms.txt). Search engines may still be allowed; see the other findings.
robots-blocks-us.t: This site asks crawlers like vibecheck to stay out
robots-blocks-us.v: Allow the 'vibecheck-visibility' user agent in robots.txt if you want a full report, or run the CLI against your own site.

robots-missing.d: Search engines crawl fine without one, but robots.txt is where crawlers look for your sitemap, and the first place AI companies' crawlers check.
robots-missing.f: My site has no robots.txt. Add one at the site root that allows everything ('User-agent: *' then 'Allow: /') and names my sitemap with a 'Sitemap: https://<my domain>/sitemap.xml' line. If my framework generates it (Next.js app/robots.ts), use that.
robots-missing.v: Open /robots.txt in a browser: it should be plain text, not your app's home page.

server-rendered.t: Content is in the raw HTML

site-unreachable.d: We couldn't load the home page, so no checks ran. Check the address and that the site is up.
site-unreachable.v: Open the address in a browser, then scan again.

sitemap-broken-urls.d: Your sitemap sends crawlers to pages that return errors or redirect. Search Console reports these, and enough of them make crawlers trust the sitemap less.
sitemap-broken-urls.f: My sitemap.xml lists URLs that don't return 200 ({excerpt}). Remove dead pages, and list redirected ones by their final URL.
sitemap-broken-urls.t: Sitemap lists pages that don't load
sitemap-broken-urls.v: Re-run this scan, or check Search Console's Pages report for 'Submitted URL not found'.

sitemap-incomplete.d: Your site links to pages your sitemap doesn't list. Crawlers can still find them by following links, but the sitemap is your statement of what matters, and pages left out of it get crawled less often.
sitemap-incomplete.f: My sitemap.xml is missing pages my site links to ({excerpt}). Generate the sitemap from my routes rather than by hand, so every public page is listed, and leave out only pages that shouldn't be found (admin, thank-you pages).
sitemap-incomplete.v: Open /sitemap.xml and check each page your navigation links to is listed.

sitemap-invalid.d: Your sitemap exists but isn't valid XML, so crawlers ignore it.
sitemap-invalid.f: My /sitemap.xml isn't valid sitemap XML ({excerpt}). Fix it so it is a standard <urlset xmlns="http://www.sitemaps.org/schemas/sitemap/0.9"> with one <url><loc>full URL</loc><lastmod>YYYY-MM-DD</lastmod></url> per page, and make sure the server sends it as XML, not as my app's HTML.
sitemap-invalid.v: Paste /sitemap.xml into Google Search Console under Sitemaps and check it reads 'Success'.

sitemap-lastmod-stale.d: Your sitemap says these pages last changed earlier than the server says they did. Crawlers use lastmod to decide what to re-read, so an old date means your changes are picked up late, or a wrong date teaches them to ignore it.
sitemap-lastmod-stale.f: The <lastmod> dates in my sitemap.xml are older than my pages ({excerpt}). Set each page's lastmod from when its content last changed (the file's git commit date or the record's updated_at), not a fixed date, and regenerate the sitemap on every deploy.
sitemap-lastmod-stale.t: Sitemap dates are older than the pages
sitemap-lastmod-stale.v: Open /sitemap.xml after your next content change and check that page's lastmod moved.

sitemap-missing.d: A sitemap is the list of pages you want found. Without one, crawlers only find what they can reach by following links, and new pages take longer to show up.
sitemap-missing.f: My site has no sitemap.xml. Generate one at /sitemap.xml listing every public page with its full URL and a <lastmod> date that changes when the page changes. Build it from my routes so new pages are added automatically (Next.js: app/sitemap.ts; Vite: a build step or vite-plugin-sitemap). Reference it from robots.txt.
sitemap-missing.v: Open /sitemap.xml: it should be XML listing your pages. Then submit it in Google Search Console under Sitemaps and check it reads 'Success'.

sitemap-not-in-robots.d: Crawlers that don't know your sitemap's address find it through a 'Sitemap:' line in robots.txt. Bing and most AI crawlers rely on it.
sitemap-not-in-robots.f: Add a line to my robots.txt: 'Sitemap: ' followed by the full URL of my sitemap (for example https://example.com/sitemap.xml).
sitemap-not-in-robots.t: robots.txt doesn't point to the sitemap
sitemap-not-in-robots.v: Open /robots.txt and check the Sitemap line is there with a full URL.

sitemap-orphans.d: These pages are in your sitemap but no page we crawled links to them. Search engines treat a page with no internal links as unimportant.
sitemap-orphans.f: These pages are in my sitemap but nothing on my site links to them: {excerpt}. Link each one from a relevant page or the footer, or take it out of the sitemap if it shouldn't be found.
sitemap-orphans.v: Re-run this scan; the pages should no longer be listed as orphans.

title-duplicate.d: Several pages have the same title, so search engines can't tell them apart and may show only one.
title-duplicate.f: These pages share a title: {excerpt}. Give each page a title that says what that page in particular is about.

title-long.d: Search results cut titles at about 60 characters, so the end of these is lost, and that's often where the brand name is.
title-long.f: Shorten these page titles to 60 characters or fewer, keeping the words people search for at the front: {excerpt}.

title-missing.d: The <title> is the blue link in search results and the name in every AI citation. Without one, search engines make one up.
title-missing.f: These pages have no <title>: {excerpt}. Give every page its own title, under 60 characters, leading with what the page is about and ending with the brand name.
title-missing.v: View source on each page and check the <title>.

titles-ok.t: Every page has a title of a sensible length

trust-missing.d: People and AI assistants both look for signs a site is a real business before recommending it: a way to get in touch, a privacy policy, who runs it, and what it costs.
trust-missing.f: My home page doesn't show {excerpt}. Add them, in the footer if nowhere else: a contact email or page, a link to the privacy policy, the company name (and registered number and address where the law asks for it), and prices or a link to pricing.
trust-missing.t: Trust details not on the page

trust-ok.t: Contact, privacy, company and pricing are on the page

viewport-missing.d: Without a viewport tag phones show the desktop layout shrunk down. Google indexes the mobile version first, so this costs rankings.
viewport-missing.f: Add <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1"> to the <head> of every page ({excerpt}).
viewport-missing.v: Open the site on a phone: text should be readable without zooming.

title: Visibility
